This page, as in many other character's pages I have viewed just today, contain "portraits" of the people the page is describing. These "portraits," created by a user named "-kay-" appear to be some kind of template which -kay- uses for all of his or her "portraits," regardless of gender. They are standing splay-footed, left arm bent and coiled into a fist, and the right arm - also in a fist - hanging to its side. In every case the arms are masculine and muscular, as are the legs, and the facial features are generic-looking and generally unsightly.

All in all, these "portraits" do an injustice to the character. And the only reason I can see to keep any of them around - particularly when there are so many very artistic versions on here by people with true talent - is if there is no portrait of that person at all. Even then, the decision to let it stand should be weighed according to whether or not it is better in a certain situation to have these cookie cutter "portraits" than to not have them on the page at all. I removed one already as it was simply so offensive to me I could not bear to look at it. Replace it if you want, but unless I am told otherwise by an admin, or unless there is a consensus leaning toward keeping them, I will remove them as I find them. These things are ridiculous to look upon, and again, do the characters they represent an injustice.

== This doesn't make any sense ==

''"This is hinted at in [[Knife of Dreams/Chapter 21|Chapter 21 of Knife of Dreams]] when they visit an Inn in Tear; "He asked Alivia whether she had gotten a good look at the fellow, but she shook her head silently. Her face was still pale. She was ferocious when she talked of what she wanted to do to ''sul'dam'', yet it seemed just hearing the accents of her native land was enough to shake her. He hoped that did not turn out to be weakness in her. She was going to help him, somehow, and he could not ''afford'' her to be weak." A literal use of the word "afford" when the reader would perceive it as figuratively."''


Is it just me, or does this interpretation seem to be a stretch? The interpretation of "he could not afford her to be weak" does not seem to be an attempt at foreshadowing or double-meaning. It makes sense in the context of Alivia's trauma, but makes no sense in a literal interpretation.
